questions.stem: Under Incoterms 2020, DPU (Delivered at Place Unloaded) and DAP (Delivered at Place) are nearly identical — except for one critical difference. What is it?
options: DPU applies to sea and inland waterway transport only; DAP covers all modes
Under DPU, the seller bears the cost and risk of unloading at the named destination; under DAP, unloading is the buyer's responsibility and risk
Under DAP, the seller must clear the goods for import; under DPU, import clearance falls to the buyer
Risk under DPU transfers at the origin terminal; risk under DAP transfers at the final named place
questions.why: DPU replaced DAT in 2020 and is the only Incoterm requiring the seller to unload at destination — making DPU more seller-onerous than DAP for exactly one operation.
questions.deepDive: DPU (formerly DAT — Delivered at Terminal) was renamed to clarify it can apply to any named place, not just a terminal. The defining distinction from DAP is unloading: under DAP, risk and cost transfer when goods are placed at the buyer's disposal on the arriving conveyance, ready for unloading. Under DPU, the seller must physically unload and deliver. In practice, a DPU seller must arrange unloading equipment, bear damage risk during that operation, and absorb the unloading fee. Exporters frequently misquote DPU when they mean DAP — a costly error when dockside crane hire and liability fall on the wrong party. DAP is generally preferred by sellers for this reason.

questions.stem: A shipper presents a 'to order' Bill of Lading endorsed in blank by the original shipper. In terms of title to the goods, what does blank endorsement legally create?
options: A non-negotiable document tied to the named consignee on the BL
A document where title vests in the issuing carrier until the goods are released
A bearer instrument — title passes to whoever physically holds the original BL
A straight BL where only the notify party can take delivery
questions.why: Blank endorsement converts a 'to order' BL into a bearer instrument — whoever possesses the original document can present it and take delivery, regardless of name.
questions.deepDive: A 'to order' BL is negotiable by nature: the consignee field reads 'to order of shipper' or 'to order of [bank]'. To transfer title, the holder endorses it — either specifically (to a named party) or in blank (no name, just a signature). Blank endorsement makes it function like bearer paper: any holder can demand delivery. This is why banks financing international trade insist on holding original BLs — they are the pledge. Losing a blank-endorsed BL is equivalent to losing cash. Electronic BLs (eBLs) on platforms like WAVE or Bolero are specifically designed to replicate negotiability while preventing physical loss. Banks will typically only release payment under an LC once they receive the original endorsed BL.

questions.stem: A shipper declares high-value electronics as 'general cargo' to obtain a carrier's lower FAK rate instead of the applicable higher commodity rate. What is the primary risk of this misdeclaration?
options: The carrier may retroactively apply the commodity rate but must honour the lower FAK liability cap
The carrier's own liability for the goods increases proportionally with the commodity rate
The shipper may face a misdeclaration surcharge and forfeit the right to claim against the carrier's standard cargo liability limits
The shipper is entitled to a refund if the commodity rate is later found inapplicable to the cargo
questions.why: Misdeclaring cargo type can trigger surcharges and — critically — allow the carrier to disclaim liability since declared cargo description was inaccurate, voiding standard protections.
questions.deepDive: FAK rates cover a wide range of cargo under one flat rate, attracting shippers moving mixed loads. When cargo is knowingly misclassified to get a lower FAK rate, the risks include: (1) a misdeclaration surcharge, sometimes 3-5x the rate difference; (2) voidance of cargo insurance if the policy is linked to declared value; (3) loss of carrier liability protection, since Hague-Visby/COGSA carrier liability is tied to the BL description. Many service contracts explicitly prohibit FAK use for specified commodities. For electronics, a single container loss can exceed $1M. Consistent misdeclaration can also trigger customs investigations, as declared cargo descriptions cross-reference trade statistics and duty calculations.

questions.stem: A forwarder consolidates cargo from multiple Dhaka exporters onto a single MAWB to Frankfurt, issuing HAWBs to each shipper. If one shipper's cargo is damaged in transit, what is the correct liability chain under the Montreal Convention?
options: The airline's liability runs to the MAWB holder (the forwarder); each shipper's claim runs against the forwarder, not the airline
The airline bears full liability directly to each HAWB shipper under the Montreal Convention
Liability is pro-rated by weight across all HAWB shippers, paid directly by the airline
HAWB shippers can bypass the forwarder and claim directly from the airline under cargo insurance subrogation
questions.why: Montreal Convention privity: the carrier's contract of carriage (the MAWB) is with the forwarder. Individual HAWB shippers have no direct claim against the airline.
questions.deepDive: The Montreal Convention 1999 governs international air cargo liability and its privity rule means the airline is liable only to its contracting party — the MAWB consignor, i.e., the forwarder acting as consolidator. Individual HAWB shippers must claim against the forwarder, who then claims against the airline on their behalf. This is why HAWB terms matter: a well-drafted HAWB passes Montreal Convention protections down (19 SDR/kg unless declared), caps the forwarder's own liability at the same limits, and preserves subrogation rights. The distinction collapses only in direct MAWB shipments where the shipper is named on the MAWB itself. Forwarders operating as NVOCCs in air are sometimes confused with this; in air, the MAWB holder has privity, full stop.

questions.stem: Bangladesh is not an RCEP member. What is the most concrete competitive disadvantage this creates for Bangladeshi RMG exporters versus RCEP members like Vietnam and Cambodia?
options: Bangladesh faces no disadvantage because EU EBA preferences more than offset RCEP membership benefits
RCEP excludes all textile and apparel categories, making non-membership irrelevant for RMG
Bangladesh benefits indirectly via its bilateral FTA with China under RCEP's MFN extension clause
RCEP members can source inputs from any member country under cumulation rules, conferring a cost and rules-of-origin advantage in intra-RCEP markets that Bangladesh cannot match
questions.why: RCEP's cumulation rules let members treat inputs from any member country as 'local' for origin purposes — dramatically lowering compliance costs and opening intra-regional supply chains Bangladesh cannot access.
questions.deepDive: RCEP covers 15 Asia-Pacific economies (ASEAN-10, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand). Its diagonal cumulation provisions mean a Vietnamese garment maker sourcing Chinese fabric and Korean synthetic yarn can count both as domestic content for rules-of-origin compliance across RCEP markets. Bangladesh, outside the bloc, must meet each market's individual origin requirements independently — sourcing fabric locally or from agreed bilateral partners. RCEP gives Vietnam and Cambodia preferential access to Chinese raw materials at lower cost, while Bangladesh competes at a structural disadvantage for intra-Asian orders. Bangladesh's push for bilateral FTA talks with ASEAN members partly reflects this gap. RCEP also creates a de facto preferential zone for intra-bloc logistics, sourcing, and investment that Bangladesh cannot tap.

questions.stem: The Wakhan Corridor — a narrow finger of Afghan territory extending east to the Chinese border — was deliberately shaped by 19th-century Great Power rivalry. What was its primary geopolitical purpose?
options: To prevent the British Indian empire and the Russian empire from sharing a common land border, maintaining a territorial buffer
To give Afghanistan direct access to China for trade along the eastern Silk Road
To provide Imperial Russia a land corridor toward the Indian Ocean, bypassing British naval dominance
To allow Persia to maintain territorial continuity with China and resist British encroachment from India
questions.why: The Wakhan Corridor was drawn in 1895 so the British and Russian empires never directly touched — Afghanistan served as the buffer strip between two expanding imperial systems.
questions.deepDive: The Wakhan Corridor is a direct legacy of the Great Game — the 19th-century imperial rivalry between Britain (protecting India) and Russia (expanding south into Central Asia). The Pamir Boundary Commission of 1895 drew the corridor's borders, assigning the narrow strip to Afghanistan (then effectively a British buffer state) to prevent a Russian-British land border. Today the corridor is 15-65km wide, borders Tajikistan, China, and Pakistan, and is one of the world's most inaccessible regions — home to Wakhi and Kyrgyz nomads. Post-2001, it gained attention as a Taliban supply route. China has built road infrastructure approaching from its side, making the corridor relevant again in Belt and Road geopolitics and cross-border security discussions.

questions.stem: The Meissner effect is a hallmark of true superconductivity, distinguishing superconductors from perfect conductors. What does it specifically involve?
options: The spontaneous emission of electric fields from the material's surface below the critical temperature
The complete expulsion of thermal energy to the environment, driving the material to absolute zero
The condensation of Cooper pairs onto the material surface, creating a quantum skin effect
The expulsion of magnetic fields from the interior of the material when cooled below the critical temperature
questions.why: The Meissner effect is the expulsion of magnetic flux from a superconductor's interior — a perfect diamagnetic response that distinguishes it from a mere perfect conductor, which would trap existing flux.
questions.deepDive: Discovered by Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld in 1933, the Meissner effect occurs because superconductors develop surface currents that exactly cancel any applied magnetic field inside the material. A perfect conductor preserves whatever magnetic flux existed when it became superconducting; a superconductor actively expels it regardless of field history — this asymmetry is captured in the London equations. Practically, the Meissner effect enables magnetic levitation (maglev trains), MRI machines, and particle accelerator beam steering. High-temperature superconductors (cuprates, discovered 1986) exhibit the effect above liquid nitrogen temperature, making them economically viable. Room-temperature superconductivity remains the holy grail of condensed matter physics — each claimed discovery (like LK-99 in 2023) triggers enormous scientific and investment attention.

questions.stem: Nobel laureate Kenzaburo Oe (Nobel Prize 1994) drew on deeply personal experience for 'A Personal Matter' (1964). What is the novel's central subject?
options: Japan's psychological reckoning with its status as the only country struck by nuclear weapons in wartime
A father's moral crisis following the birth of his brain-damaged son — whether to accept or abandon the child
The long psychological shadow of Japan's colonial rule over Korea, told through a Japanese-Korean friendship
A soldier's haunted guilt over atrocities committed during the Imperial Army's campaign in China
questions.why: Oe's novel is autobiographical: his son Hikari was born with a brain abnormality, and the book explores the protagonist Bird's temptation to let the infant die versus accepting and raising him.
questions.deepDive: Kenzaburo Oe (1935-2023) won the Nobel Prize 'for poetic force creating an imagined world, where life and myth condense to form a disconcerting picture of the human predicament today.' 'A Personal Matter' (Kojinteki na Taiken) was written after his son Hikari was born with an encephalocele in 1963. The protagonist Bird must choose between a romanticised escape to Africa and confronting his responsibility as a father. Oe chose to care for Hikari, who became a celebrated composer of classical music. Unlike Mishima's aesthetics of death and national mythology, Oe's moral framework is rooted in life's radical imperfection and the ethics of caregiving. The novel sits alongside 'The Silent Cry' as Oe's most essential work.

questions.stem: HBO's 'The Wire' (2002-2008), created by David Simon, is unique in that each season takes a different Baltimore institution as its thematic lens. Which option correctly matches a season to its focus?
options: Season 2 — Baltimore City Hall and municipal politics
Season 3 — the Baltimore public school system
Season 4 — the Baltimore docks and the longshoremen's union
Season 2 — the Baltimore docks and the longshoremen's union
questions.why: Season 2 focused on the Port of Baltimore and the longshoremen's union — a deliberate shift from the drug war to show how deindustrialisation devastates working-class port communities.
questions.deepDive: David Simon structured each Wire season around a different institution: Season 1 (drug trade/police), Season 2 (the docks/longshoremen — smuggling and labour decline), Season 3 (city government/police reform, including the 'Hamsterdam' experiment), Season 4 (public school system — arguably the show's finest), Season 5 (the Baltimore Sun and journalism). Season 2 is frequently cited as the most underrated: it used container smuggling — including the discovery of bodies in a shipping container — as a metaphor for globalisation hollowing out blue-collar port work. The show is widely taught in sociology, criminology, and media studies as rare TV of genuine literary ambition. David Simon drew on his book 'The Corner' and reporting at The Baltimore Sun.

questions.stem: At the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference, John Maynard Keynes proposed a radically different international monetary system from what was ultimately adopted. What was the central feature of his rejected proposal?
options: A gold-backed single world currency managed by a neutral supranational central bank without US veto
Fixed exchange rates pegged to sterling, with the UK acting as global reserve manager in place of the US
An International Clearing Union issuing a supranational currency ('bancor') with symmetrical adjustment obligations on both debtor and creditor nations
A system of bilateral trade-balancing agreements between major trading nations, bypassing multilateral institutions
questions.why: Keynes's 'bancor' plan would have penalised surplus countries (like the US) as well as deficit countries — fundamentally different from the adopted White Plan, which put adjustment burden only on debtors.
questions.deepDive: Bretton Woods was a contest between Keynes's International Clearing Union (ICU) and Harry Dexter White's IMF plan. Keynes's bancor was a supranational bookkeeping currency; crucially, countries running persistent surpluses would be charged interest — forcing them to spend or lend rather than accumulate indefinitely. White's plan (which prevailed) made the US dollar the anchor, gave the US an effective IMF veto, and placed adjustment pressure mainly on deficit countries. Keynes's system would have been more symmetrical but stripped US monetary sovereignty. The asymmetry Keynes feared — surplus nations accumulating while deficits adjust painfully — is precisely the dynamic that caused the 1960s 'dollar glut,' the 1971 Nixon shock, and recurring global imbalances through today. Keynes is widely considered to have lost the negotiation but won the intellectual argument.
